short_definition: Analysis paralysis is overthinking a decision so much, by endlessly gathering information or comparing options, that you delay or never make a choice, often at real cost.
explanation: Analysis paralysis happens when gathering more information becomes a substitute for deciding. It is often driven by fear of choosing wrong, perfectionism or simply having too many options. Each new piece of research raises new questions, so the decision keeps getting pushed back. Psychologist Barry Schwartz's 'paradox of choice' describes a related idea: more options can make choosing harder and less satisfying.

Not deciding is a decision too, and it has costs. Money sits idle, a business idea never launches, or a job offer expires. Recognizing analysis paralysis helps you weigh the cost of waiting against the value of more research.

Some decisions do deserve deep research, especially high-stakes ones that are hard to reverse. A practical approach is to sort decisions into reversible and hard-to-reverse. For reversible ones, set a deadline, limit the criteria and accept a 'good enough' choice. Don't use this as an excuse to rush major financial or legal decisions without proper advice.
example: Illustrative example: Leo has spent three months comparing 12 budgeting apps and still hasn't started a budget. He sets a rule: shortlist 3 apps, judge them on 3 criteria (cost, bank syncing and ease of use), and decide by Sunday. He picks one, starts tracking his spending that week, and knows he can switch later because the choice is easy to reverse.
common_mistake: Treating every decision as high-stakes and irreversible, for example giving the choice of a note-taking app the same research effort as a mortgage.
title: Analysis Paralysis
